rounds.verdict: A sound pull-back reveal concept, undermined by mis-cut fragment layers and no purposeful layer story — do not publish as-is.
filmIssues: The pull-back idea is right for the scene — tight on the waiting children, then revealing the whole library and its open door as their destination — but in execution it reads as little more than a plain centred zoom-out, no better in storytelling than the baseline move it is scored against.

The cut-outs do not match their names: cut-1 'library' is a tiny 0.050 x 0.161 slice at lower-left foreground, and cut-2 'children' is a single narrow 0.035-wide child, not the building or the whole queue. The remaining children and the building stay on the painted background.

Because those two fragments share driftY -0.03 and scale 0.96 at different depths, individual children are pulled slightly away from the queue they belong to. At contact-sheet size the group still holds together broadly, but the split is conceptually wrong and risks doubled edges / a ghost on the painted-over spots behind the moved fragments.

The t=0 frame at zoom 1.4 is an awkward opening picture: the foreground is pushed toward the bottom edge, the right-hand trishaws crowd the frame edge, and the library — the subject of the caption — is not yet readable as a whole. The t=1 full-plate frame is a good dwell picture, with the border, building, children and trishaws all comfortably inside.

No entrance or layer journey carries the 'arrival' story: the children never advance toward the door, the trishaws do not arrive, and the blank plaque / doorway is never specifically discovered. Dust is fitting and subtle for an archive print and does not disturb the 1950s lithograph style.

plan.rationale: A quiet beginning of arrival: the camera opens tight on the waiting schoolchildren and reveals outward and upward to the whole red-brick library, so the open door is discovered as their destination.

rounds.verdict: Do not publish as-is: a timid generic pull-back that does not clearly express the opening-day reveal, despite a good final dwell frame.
filmIssues: The rendered move is effectively a plain centred pull-back: the six frames differ only by a slight scale change, with no clear staged reveal from the children/queue to the library as a whole.

The opening at nominal zoom 1.38 is damped/timid in the render - the building already reads almost complete at t=0, so the intended tight start on the children-doorway axis is not felt, and the poster border is awkwardly clipped without a purposeful close-up to justify it.

The two cut-outs are tiny mis-cut fragments (cut-1 and cut-2 are narrow slivers, not the whole library or children group); at depths 0.6/0.8 camera parallax can separate them from the painted plate and produce doubled edges/ghosting around the doorway/children.
No layer entrance or drift gives the queue a sense of arrival or directs attention to the blank plaque/door; the story 'a door open to anyone' is not expressed by the motion.
The final full-plate frame is a good dwell image and dust is fitting and subtle for the archive print, but that alone does not lift it above a generic move.

rounds.verdict: A coherent, clean pull-back to a good final plate, but the opening is not tight or specific enough for the reveal to carry the story at publishable level.
filmIssues: The pull-back is visible but timid in execution: the t=0 frame already shows the whole building, children and trishaws, so it never reads as genuinely tight on the doorway/children/plaque axis and the reveal to the full plate feels like a plain centred zoom-out rather than a purposeful story move.

Because the first and last frames are compositionally very similar, the opening picture does not create a distinct starting point and the final dwell frame gains little from the journey; the move expresses 'showing the building' more than 'a library door open to anyone' with its waiting queue.

Dust is barely perceptible in the frames and adds little archive atmosphere; no tearing, doubled edges or obvious ghosting is visible from the pinned fragment layers, and no layer clips the frame awkwardly.
